name: Rae Thorne
epithet: Carter of the last cart to the foot of the Steps
appearance: Twenty-seven, or near it, and strong through the shoulders in the way that comes from hauling rather than from Grace. She has a fair, open face with the wind's colour in it, grey-green eyes that stay on the road, and honey-brown hair that the hood of her cloak gives up holding, so that it falls loose past her shoulders and curls in the damp. She wears a dark hooded wool cloak pinned at the throat with a plain iron clasp over a linen shirt the colour of old cream, and a small brass bell hangs on a cord at her belt and rings whenever the cart jolts, which she never seems to hear. She drives the last cart up the Holloway to the foot of the Thousand Steps, talks to her oxen in whole sentences and to knights hardly at all, and looked at Darrow's hurt leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel.
portrait_alt: Portrait of Rae Thorne: a young woman of about twenty-seven with honey-brown hair falling loose past her shoulders, grey-green eyes and a small warm smile, in a dark hooded wool cloak pinned with a plain iron clasp over a cream linen shirt, before the stone and timber houses of a mountain village.
last_seen_doing: On the gate-ward's bench on the wall-walk at noon, having sat down at one end of it so that Darrow would sit at the other, because she had seen his leg shaking.
now: In the House, with her cart and two oxen at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps, where six grey cloaks have come in and one of them sits on her cart with his boots on the board. Darrow told her to go down while the road was open; she stayed, and said the first two names on the list rode up in her cart. Her oxen, she says, will stand all winter.
story_so_far: She drove the last cart of Darrow's road north, a salt-cart off the Holloway with its load left at the landing to make room for two knights and a leg that was not there, talking to her oxen the whole day and to her passengers not at all. When Hollis started on her she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather. At the foot of the Steps she looked at Darrow's leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, rang the bell at her belt three times, and a bell answered from the cloud; the lay brothers who came down with the litter called her Rae, and the one thing she said to Darrow all day was that they would count him up and he should not help. Seven weeks after Darrow's Binding she was in the taproom at Coldmere with the House's salt on her cart when the Confessors read out their list of the Faithless at Saint Ysolde's. She drove the Holloway in the dark ahead of them, climbed the Steps before the bell, and told the winch-brothers, who told the kitchen; her cart and oxen wait at the winch-house below, at the foot of the Steps. When the grey cloaks came in three bells early and one of them put his boots up on her cart, she stood on the gate wall beside Darrow, said "Aye" to every reason he gave her to go, and let the road shut: the first two names on that list, she said, rode up in her cart.

quote.text: The first two names on that list rode up in my cart.

known_facts.fact: She drove the last cart of the road north, a salt-cart off the Holloway, its load left at the landing to make room for two knights and a leg that was not there.
She talked to her oxen the whole of the last day and to her passengers not at all, and when Hollis started on her past the second milestone she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather.
A small brass bell hangs on a cord at her belt and rings when the cart jolts; at the foot of the Steps she rang it three times, hard, and after a while a bell answered from the cloud.
She looked at Darrow's leg once, the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel: a thing that would have to be seen to, and not by her.
known_facts.evidence: the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel: a thing that would have to be seen to, and not by her

known_facts.fact: The first of the lay brothers coming down with the litter called her Rae, as if her name were a thing you could lean on.
known_facts.evidence: as if her name were a thing you could lean on

known_facts.fact: The one thing she said to Darrow in the whole of that day, as they lifted him: 'They'll count you up. Don't help.'
known_facts.evidence: They'll count you up. Don't help.

known_facts.fact: By Wren's account she was in the taproom at the inn in Coldmere with the House's salt on her cart when the Confessors' list was read out, and heard every name.
She drove the Holloway in the dark ahead of the grey cloaks, came up the Steps before the bell, and told the winch-brothers, who told the kitchen.

Her cart stands at the winch-house at the foot of the Steps with its shafts up and two oxen in the snow; Darrow knew it from the infirmary window as the cart he had ridden the last of the Holloway in.
Wren's ledger counts one cart at the winch-house, Thorne's, and one load waiting on the cage.
At Mother Ione's council she said the list was read slow, so the room could count; and the room counted.

On the stair after the council she stopped one step above Darrow, eye to eye, and asked whether he rode a grey at the ford. When he said yes and asked why, she went on up without answering; the bell at her belt rang once at the turn.
When Darrow asked to be sent down the Steps before the grey cloaks came, she said from the door that down is where they are: the first thing she had said in the council that was not an answer.

From the gate wall at noon, through Sister Pell's glass, Darrow watched a grey cloak walk round her cart at the winch-house, climb onto the box and put his boots up on the board; she had not asked for the glass.

Darrow told her to go down while the rest of the grey cloaks were an hour out, ask the man off her box and be on the road to Coldmere by dark, and that once they had the cage she would be up there till the thaw; she said "Aye" to all of it. When he said he had asked fifteen times to go down those steps and she could walk down them today, she did not say aye.
known_facts.evidence: She did not say aye to that.

known_facts.fact: When the five were in at the winch-house she pinned her cloak at the throat with its iron clasp and drew up her hood; when Darrow said that had been her road, she said the first two names on that list rode up in her cart.
known_facts.evidence: The first two names on that list rode up in my cart.

known_facts.fact: Her oxen have names; asked to tell Darrow them, she said they know them.
Reminded that Hollis cursed everything on the road the day she drove him, she said he did the oxen before her, and something came and went at the corner of her mouth that was for the oxen.
known_facts.evidence: He did the oxen before me.

known_facts.fact: Of her oxen at the winch-house with a grey cloak on her cart: they'll stand; a mule won't stand at the winch-house, and an ox will stand all winter.

When Darrow's knee began to shake from the standing, she sat down at one end of the gate-ward's bench, and he sat at the other before he had decided to; then she said, once, to the valley, that his leg was shaking.

relationships.label: the knight she drove to the foot of the Steps
relationships.note: She looked at his leg once the way a carter looks at a cracked wheel, rang for the litter, and said one thing to him all day; seven weeks after the Binding he knew her cart from the infirmary window and had not forgotten it. When the grey cloaks came in, he told her from the gate wall to go while the road was open, and she let it shut.

relationships.label: the old knight who cursed her from her own cart
relationships.note: When he started on her past the second milestone she said 'Aye' as if he had remarked on the weather, and the cart went on.

relationships.label: the runner who carried her news into the hall
relationships.note: Wren told the infirmary hall that Rae had heard the list read at Coldmere, driven through the dark ahead of the grey cloaks and climbed the Steps before the bell.

deeper: She says a thing once, and "Aye" does the work of a paragraph.
